label: thm:algebraic-commutativity
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:algebraic-commutativity}
Let \(\Bbbk\) be a field of characteristic zero. Every associative
algebraic \(n\)-valued monoid on \(\mathbb P^1_{\Bbbk}\) with a strong two-sided
unit is commutative.
head: environment
name: Commutativity of \(n\)-valued monoids on \(\Pp^1_{\kfield}\

label: thm:formal-commutativity
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:formal-commutativity}
Let \(R\) be a reduced commutative \(\mathbb Q\)-algebra. Let
\[
 P(Z;x,y)=Z^n-\theta_1(x,y)Z^{n-1}+\cdots+(-1)^n\theta_n(x,y)
 \in R[[x,y]][Z]
\]
be an associative one-dimensional formal \(n\)-valued multiplication with
strong two-sided unit
\[
 P(Z;x,0)=(Z-x)^n,
 \qquad
 P(Z;0,y)=(Z-y)^n.
\]
Then
\[
 P(Z;x,y)=P(Z;y,x),
\] i.e., the \(n\)-valued multiplication is commutative.
Under the same associativity and unit hypotheses over an arbitrary commutative
\(\mathbb Q\)-algebra, the coefficients of \(P(Z;x,y)-P(Z;y,x)\) belong to
the nilradical of \(R\).
head: environment
name: Commutativity of \(n\)-valued formal groups over a reduced base

label: thm:cyclicity
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:cyclicity}
Let \(R\) be a commutative \(\mathbb Q\)-algebra which is an integral domain,
and let \(P(Z;x,y)\in R[[x,y]][Z]\) define an associative one-dimensional
formal \(n\)-valued multiplication with a strong two-sided unit. Then \(P\)
is strongly isomorphic over \(R\) to the \(d\)-fold diagonal of
\(\mathbb G_m\), for a unique divisor \(m\mid n\), where \(d=n/m\). Equivalently,
there is a strong coordinate \(B(t)=t+O(t^2)\in R[[t]]\) for which
\[
 \prod_{\nu=1}^{n}\left(W-B(z_\nu(x,y))\right)
 =p_m\bigl(W;B(x),B(y)\bigr)^d.
\]
More precisely, \(m\) is both the differential order (the rank) of the
generator and the number of distinct generic roots of \(P\).  The top
coefficient of the generator is
\[
 a_m(t)=\frac{m^m}{m!}t^{m-1}A(t),
 \qquad A(t)\in1+tR[[t]].
\]
There is a unique \(H(t)\in1+tR[[t]]\) satisfying
\(H(t)+mtH'(t)=A(t)^{-1/m}\).
Writing \(A(t)^{-1/m}=\sum_{k\ge0}g_kt^k\), the strong coordinate may be
chosen explicitly as
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 B(t)&=tH(t)^m
 =\frac1{m!}\left(\int_0^t a_m(u)^{-1/m}\,\mathop{}\!\mathrm d u\right)^m\\
 &=t\left(\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{g_k}{1+mk}t^k\right)^m.
 \end{aligned}
\]
The integral is formal; its \(m\)-th power is independent of the root chosen.
If \(E=B^{-1}\), then after adjoining \(m\)-th roots and a primitive
\(m\)-th root of unity the distinct branches are
\[
 z_j(x,y)=E\left(
 \left(B(x)^{1/m}+\zeta_m^jB(y)^{1/m}\right)^m
 \right),
 \qquad j=0,\ldots,m-1,
\]
and each occurs with multiplicity \(d\).  In particular,
\(\operatorname{Disc}_Z(P)\ne0\) if and only if \(m=n\); the discriminant-zero cases are
exactly the proper diagonals \(d>1\).
head: environment
name: Classification of \(n\)-valued formal groups over an integral domain \(\mathbb Q\)-algebra

title: Corollary
body_md:
\label[corollary]{cor:divisor-count}
Under the hypotheses of \cref{thm:cyclicity}, the strong-isomorphism classes
of associative one-dimensional formal \(n\)-valued multiplications with a
strong two-sided unit are in bijection with the positive divisors of \(n\).
In particular, there are exactly \(\tau(n)\) such classes, where \(\tau(n)\) is the number of positive divisors of \(n\).
head: environment

title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Homogeneity of the law gives \(a_i(t)=c_i t^{i-1}\) for its generator
coefficients. Thus \(A(t)=1\) in \cref{thm:cyclicity}, so \(H(t)=1\) and
\(B(t)=t\). The classification identity therefore holds in the original
coordinate, and uniqueness of \(m\) follows from the same theorem.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
An \emph{algebraic \(n\)-valued monoid with a strong unit on
\(\mathbb P^1_{\Bbbk}\)} is a rational map
\[
 \mu:\mathbb P^1_{\Bbbk}\times\mathbb P^1_{\Bbbk}
 \dashrightarrow
 \operatorname{Sym}^n(\mathbb P^1_{\Bbbk})\cong\mathbb P^n_{\Bbbk}
\]
which is associative as a rational map and has a strong unit
\(e\in\mathbb P^1(\Bbbk)\). The unit condition means that \(\mu\) is defined at
the generic points of \(\{e\}\times\mathbb P^1\) and
\(\mathbb P^1\times\{e\}\), and that its restrictions there are the diagonal
degree-\(n\) divisors. Thus, after flattening symmetric powers,
\[
 (x*y)*z=x*(y*z)
 \quad\text{as rational maps to }\operatorname{Sym}^{n^2}(\mathbb P^1),
\]
\[
 x*e=e*x=\mathopen{[}x,\ldots,x\mathclose{]}.
\]
An algebraic \(n\)-valued group is an algebraic \(n\)-valued monoid equipped
with a rational inversion satisfying the usual multivalued inverse condition.
The commutativity theorem concerns the monoid before an inversion is chosen.
head: environment

label: eq:strong-isomorphism
title: Definition
body_md:
\label[definition]{def:strong}
Let \(P(W; X, Y)\) and \(Q(W;X,Y)\) be monic formal \(n\)-valued laws, and let
\[
 B(t)=t+O(t^2)\in R[[t]].
\]
Thus \(B(0)=0\), \(B'(0)=1\), and \(B\) has a compositional inverse.
The series \(B\) is a \emph{strong isomorphism} from \(P\) to \(Q\) if
\begin{equation}\label{eq:strong-isomorphism}
 \prod_{\nu=1}^n
 \left(W-B\bigl(z_\nu(x,y)\bigr)\right)
 =Q\bigl(W;B(x),B(y)\bigr),
\end{equation} where, as usual, \(z_\nu(x, y)\) denotes formal roots of the polynomial \(P(z; x, y)\) with respect to \(z\).
The left-hand side of \eqref{eq:strong-isomorphism} is a polynomial in \(W\) with coefficients in
\(R[[x,y]]\), interpreted by the preceding convention for symmetric formal
series; every branch \(z_\nu(x, y)\) is counted with its multiplicity. Since \(B(t)\) has a compositional inverse, distinct branches remain distinct after applying \(B(t)\): each branch is repeated the same number of times in the transformed polynomial as in the original polynomial.  \Cref{def:strong} is equivalent to
Buchstaber's;
see \parencite[Definition~1.3]{Buchstaber1975} and
\parencite[Lemma~1.3]{Kholodov1982}.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label[lemma]{lem:commuting-shifts}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*]
\item Let \(X\) be a set equipped with an associative \(n\)-valued multiplication
\[
 \mu:X\times X\longrightarrow\operatorname{Sym}^n(X)
\]
and a strong two-sided unit \(e\). Fix a field \(\Bbbk\) of characteristic
zero. For each \(a\in X\), define the normalized left shift on functions
\(f:X\to\Bbbk\) by
\[
 (\mathcal L_a f)(x)=\frac1n\sum_{z\in\mu(a,x)}f(z),
\]
where the sum counts multiplicities. The multiplication \(\mu\) is
commutative if and only if its normalized left shifts commute pairwise:
\[
 \mathcal L_a\mathcal L_b=\mathcal L_b\mathcal L_a
 \qquad\text{for all }a,b\in X.
\]

\item Suppose that either \(\mu\) is an associative algebraic \(n\)-valued
multiplication on \(\mathbb P^1_\Bbbk\) over a field \(\Bbbk\) of characteristic
zero, or \(P(Z;x,y)\in R[[x,y]][Z]\) defines an associative one-dimensional
formal \(n\)-valued multiplication over a commutative \(\mathbb Q\)-algebra
\(R\). In either case, assume that \(0\) is a strong two-sided unit.
The multiplication is commutative if and only if its normalized left shifts
commute on rational functions \(\Bbbk(t)\), respectively formal power series
\(R[[t]]\). The commutation identities are understood in \(\Bbbk(a,b,t)\),
respectively \(R[[a,b,t]]\), for independent parameters \(a,b\).
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Commuting-shift criterion

title: Proof
body_md:
\textup{(i)} Suppose first that the normalized left shifts commute. The strong-unit
identity gives
\[
 (\mathcal L_a\mathcal L_bf)(e)
 =(\mathcal L_bf)(a)
 =\frac1n\sum_{z\in\mu(b,a)}f(z).
\]
Interchanging \(a\) and \(b\) and using commutation yields
\[
 \sum_{z\in\mu(a,b)}f(z)=\sum_{z\in\mu(b,a)}f(z)
\]
for every \(f:X\to\Bbbk\). Taking \(f\) to be the indicator function
of each singleton shows that every element occurs with the same multiplicity
in the two multisets. Hence \(\mu(a,b)=\mu(b,a)\).

Conversely, suppose that \(\mu\) is commutative. Then
\[
 \mathcal L_a\mathcal L_b
 =\frac1n\sum_{c\in\mu(b,a)}\mathcal L_c
 =\frac1n\sum_{c\in\mu(a,b)}\mathcal L_c
 =\mathcal L_b\mathcal L_a.
\]
The first and last equalities follow from associativity, and the middle
equality follows from commutativity.

\textup{(ii)} In the one-dimensional algebraic and formal settings, the same
evaluation argument applies with \(f(t)=t^j\), \(1\le j\le n\), whenever
the left shifts commute on rational or formal functions, respectively.
Equality of these power sums and Newton's identities give equality of the
monic branch polynomials, hence commutativity of the multiplication.
The converse follows from the same associativity identity used in
\textup{(i)}.
head: environment

label: eq:coproduct
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Trace transformation and generalized shifts

label: eq:rational-coassociativity
title: Proof
body_md:
In the basis \(1,Z,\ldots,Z^{n-1}\), the operator \(\operatorname{mult}_Z\) is represented by
the companion matrix of \(\widehat P\).  Over a splitting field its
eigenvalues are the elements of \(x*y\), counted with multiplicity.  Hence
\(\operatorname{Tr}(\operatorname{mult}_{f(Z)})=\sum_{z\in x*y}f(z)\) and
\eqref{eq:coproduct} defines the stated rational function.

Associativity gives the coassociativity identity
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-coassociativity}
 \frac1{n^2}\sum_{u\in x*y}\sum_{v\in u*z}f(v)
 =\frac1{n^2}\sum_{u\in y*z}\sum_{v\in x*u}f(v)
 \quad\text{in }\Bbbk(x,y,z),
\end{equation}
because its two sides are one \(n^2\)-th of the trace over \((x*y)*z\) and
\(x*(y*z)\), respectively. We call \(\Delta\) the rational trace
comultiplication of the law: coassociativity is understood as the identity
\eqref{eq:rational-coassociativity} in \(\Bbbk(x,y,z)\). Its target is
\(\Bbbk(x,y)=\operatorname{Frac}(\Bbbk(x)\otimes_{\Bbbk}\Bbbk(y))\).
Setting either input equal to \(0\) gives \eqref{eq:shift-unit}; evaluation
\(f\mapsto f(0)\) is defined only for rational functions regular at \(0\).
The same associativity identity with inputs
\((a,t,b)\) identifies the sums defining \(\mathcal L_a\mathcal R_bf\) and \(\mathcal R_b\mathcal L_af\).  Thus
\(\mathcal L_a\mathcal R_b=\mathcal R_b\mathcal L_a\).
head: environment

label: eq:local-trace-family
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Trace coefficients are differential operators

title: Proof
body_md:
The trace family is well defined for every \(f=g/h\in K\). Indeed,
\(\mathcal A/s\mathcal A\simeq K[\delta]/(\delta^n)\), where
\(\delta=Z-t\). In this quotient, \(h(Z)=h(t)+\delta u\) for some \(u\),
so it is invertible: \(h(t)\ne0\) and \(\delta\) is nilpotent.
Since \(\mathcal A\) is finite free over \(K[[s]]\), the matrix of
multiplication by \(h(Z)\) has determinant with nonzero constant term.
It is therefore invertible over \(K[[s]]\), and \(h(Z)\) is a unit in
\(\mathcal A\).

Fix \(r\geq0\), put \(R_r=K[s]/(s^{r+1})\) and
\(\mathcal A_r=R_r[Z]/(Q)\), and write \(\delta=Z-t\).  For some
\(H\in K[[s]][\delta]\), the relation in \(\mathcal A_r\) is
\(Q(t+\delta;s)=\delta^n+sH=0\).  Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:nilpotent-delta}
 \delta^{n(r+1)}=(-sH)^{r+1}=0
 \qquad\text{in }\mathcal A_r,
\end{equation}
because \(s^{r+1}=0\) in \(R_r\).

Taylor's formula is therefore finite in \(\mathcal A_r\):
\begin{equation}\label{eq:finite-taylor}
 f(Z)=f(t+\delta)
 =\sum_{j=0}^{n(r+1)-1}
 \frac{f^{(j)}(t)}{j!}\,\delta^j.
\end{equation}
For a rational function this identity follows by applying the polynomial
Taylor formula to its numerator and expanding its denominator. The latter is
invertible modulo the nilpotent element \(\delta\).
Taking one \(n\)-th of the trace of multiplication by both sides yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:trace-taylor}
 \mathcal T_sf(t)
 \equiv
 \sum_{j=0}^{n(r+1)-1}c_j(s,t)f^{(j)}(t)
 \pmod{s^{r+1}},
 \qquad
 c_j(s,t)
 =\frac{1}{n\,j!}
 \operatorname{Tr}_{\mathcal A_r/R_r}\bigl(\operatorname{mult}_{\delta^j}\bigr)
 \in R_r.
\end{equation}
Although \(\delta^j\) depends on \(Z\), its trace does not: the trace of an
\(R_r\)-linear endomorphism lies in the base ring \(R_r\). Taking the
coefficient of \(s^r\) in \eqref{eq:trace-taylor} expresses \(A_r\) as a
finite sum of operators \(a_j(t)\partial_t^j\), with
\(a_j(t)\in\Bbbk(t)\), and proves the assertion.
head: environment

label: thm:schur-amitsur
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:schur-amitsur}
Let \(\Bbbk\) be a field of characteristic zero, let
\(K\) be either \(\Bbbk(t)\) or \(\Bbbk((t))\), and put
\(\mathcal D_K=K\langle\partial_t\rangle\). If
\(D\in\mathcal D_K\setminus\Bbbk\), then its centralizer
\[
 C_{\mathcal D_K}(D)
 =\{A\in\mathcal D_K:[A,D]=0\}
\]
is commutative.
head: environment
name: Schur--Amitsur centralizer theorem

title: Proof
body_md:
Choose a projective coordinate in which the unit is \(0\), and use the affine
chart containing it.  At the generic point of this chart, divide the polynomial
\(P(Z;x,y)\) by its leading coefficient and define the generalized shifts
\(\mathcal L_a,\mathcal R_b\) by \eqref{eq:shifts}. The identity
\(0*t=[t,\ldots,t]\) controls the expansion of \(\mathcal L_a\) at \(a=0\), while
\(t*0=[t,\ldots,t]\) controls the expansion of \(\mathcal R_b\) at \(b=0\). The
coefficients of the corresponding monic representatives are regular in these
parameters at zero: the rational map is defined at the generic points of the
two unit divisors and lands in the chosen affine output chart there. We
therefore have presentations
\begin{equation}\label{eq:operator-expansions}
 \mathcal L_a=\sum_{r\geq0}a^rD_r(t,\partial_t),
 \qquad
 \mathcal R_b=\sum_{s\geq0}b^sE_s(t,\partial_t)
\end{equation}
as formal operator families on \(\Bbbk(t)\), where \(D_r\) and \(E_s\) are
certain differential polynomials with rational coefficients.

Apply \cref{prop:trace-differential} to
\(Q(Z;s)=\widehat P(Z;s,t)\) and to
\(Q(Z;s)=\widehat P(Z;t,s)\).  The unit identity
\eqref{eq:unit-polynomial} supplies the required specialization at \(s=0\),
so
\begin{equation}\label{eq:coefficients-diff}
 D_r,E_s\in\Bbbk(t)\langle\partial_t\rangle
 \qquad\text{for all }r,s\geq0.
\end{equation}

By \cref{prop:coalgebra}, associativity gives \(\mathcal L_a\mathcal R_b=\mathcal R_b\mathcal L_a\).
Substitute \eqref{eq:operator-expansions} and compare the coefficient of
\(a^rb^s\).  This gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:mixed-coefficients}
 [D_r,E_s]=0
 \qquad\text{for all }r,s\geq0.
\end{equation}

Since \(\mathcal R_b1=1\), comparison of coefficients gives \(E_s1=0\) for
every \(s\ge1\). Put \(f_0(t)=t\) and
\(H(t,b)=(\mathcal R_bf_0)(t)-t\). The left-unit identity gives \(H(0,b)=b\),
so \(H\) is a nonzero rational function. Its formal expansion at \(b=0\)
is therefore nonzero, since a rational function with zero expansion is zero.
As \(E_0=\operatorname{id}\), the constant term cancels, leaving
\begin{equation}\label{eq:nonzero-shift-coefficient}
 H(t,b)=\sum_{s\ge1}b^s(E_sf_0)(t).
\end{equation}
Thus at least one coefficient \(E_{s_0}f_0\), with \(s_0\ge1\), is
nonzero. Consequently, \(E_{s_0}\ne0\), and \(E_{s_0}1=0\) shows that
it is not scalar.

Every \(D_r\) belongs, by \eqref{eq:mixed-coefficients}, to the centralizer of
\(E_{s_0}\) in \(\Bbbk(t)\langle\partial_t\rangle\). By \cref{thm:schur-amitsur}, that centralizer is
commutative.  Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{eq:left-coefficients-commute}
 [D_r,D_q]=0
 \qquad\text{for all }r,q\geq0.
\end{equation}
It follows first as a formal identity at \((a,b)=(0,0)\). Expansion in the
local parameters is injective on rational functions regular there, so this is
an identity of rational operator families: all left generalized shifts
commute,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:left-shifts-commute}
 \mathcal L_a\mathcal L_b=\mathcal L_b\mathcal L_a.
\end{equation}

By \cref{lem:commuting-shifts}\textup{(ii)}, the multiplication is
commutative on the dense
open set where the correspondences and their affine branch polynomials are
defined.  Hence the two rational maps \(\mu(x,y)\) and \(\mu(y,x)\) to the
separated variety \(\operatorname{Sym}^n(\mathbb P^1)\) agree as rational maps.  This proves
\cref{thm:algebraic-commutativity}.
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md:
\label[proposition]{prop:formal-shift-coefficients}
Let \(\Bbbk\) be a field of characteristic zero and let
\(P(Z;x,y)\in\Bbbk[[x,y]][Z]\) be an associative formal
\(n\)-valued multiplication satisfying \eqref{eq:formal-unit}. Then
\[
 \mathcal L_a=\sum_{r\ge0}a^rD_r(t,\partial_t),
 \qquad
 \mathcal R_b=\sum_{s\ge0}b^sE_s(t,\partial_t),
\]
where
\[
 D_r,E_s\in\Bbbk((t))\langle\partial_t\rangle.
\]
Moreover,
\[
 [D_r,E_s]=0
 \qquad\text{for all }r,s\ge0,
\]
and, for every \(f\in\Bbbk[[t]]\),
\[
 \mathcal L_0=\mathcal R_0=\operatorname{id},
 \qquad
 (\mathcal L_af)(0)=(\mathcal R_af)(0)=f(a).
\]
head: environment
name: Formal shift coefficients

title: Proof
body_md:
For \(r\ge0\), reduce \(P(Z;a,t)\) modulo \(a^{r+1}\) and work in
\[
 \mathcal A_r=
 \bigl(\Bbbk[[t]][a]/(a^{r+1})\bigr)[Z]/(P(Z;a,t)).
\]
Writing \(\delta=Z-t\), the unit identity gives
\(\delta^n\in a\mathcal A_r\), hence \(\delta^{n(r+1)}=0\). The finite
Taylor expansion used in \cref{prop:trace-differential}, followed by the
normalized trace and extraction of the coefficient of \(a^r\), gives
\(D_r\in\Bbbk[[t]]\langle\partial_t\rangle\), of order at most
\(n(r+1)-1\). Applying the same argument to \(P(Z;t,b)\) gives the
assertion for \(E_s\). Associativity identifies the branch sums defining
\(\mathcal L_a\mathcal R_bf\) and \(\mathcal R_b\mathcal L_af\) in \(\Bbbk[[a,b,t]]\).
Comparing coefficients of \(a^rb^s\) gives \([D_r,E_s]=0\). The remaining
identities follow from the strong two-sided unit.
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
\label[corollary]{cor:formal-field-commutativity}
Let \(\Bbbk\) be a field of characteristic zero. Every associative
one-dimensional formal \(n\)-valued multiplication over \(\Bbbk\) with a
strong two-sided unit is commutative.
head: environment
name: Formal commutativity over a field

title: Proof
body_md:
For \(f_0(t)=t\), the series \((\mathcal R_bf_0)(t)\) belongs to
\(\Bbbk[[t,b]]\), so coefficient extraction commutes with evaluation at
\(t=0\). The unit identity therefore gives \((E_1f_0)(0)=1\).
Moreover, \(E_1(1)=0\), since \(\mathcal R_b1=1\), so \(E_1\) is nonscalar.
By \cref{prop:formal-shift-coefficients}, every \(D_r\) belongs to its
centralizer in \(\Bbbk((t))\langle\partial_t\rangle\), which is
commutative by \cref{thm:schur-amitsur}. Hence all \(D_r\) commute, and
therefore so do the left shifts on \(\Bbbk[[t]]\).
\Cref{lem:commuting-shifts}\textup{(ii)} proves the claim.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write
\[
 \delta_i(x,y)
 =\theta_i(x,y)-\theta_i(y,x)
 =\sum_{r,s\ge0}c_{i,r,s}x^ry^s,
 \qquad c_{i,r,s}\in R.
\]
We prove that every coefficient \(c_{i,r,s}\) belongs to the nilradical of
\(R\).

Fix a prime ideal \(\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec} R\), and put
\[
 \kappa(\mathfrak p)=\operatorname{Frac}(R/\mathfrak p).
\]
Let
\[
 \lambda_{\mathfrak p}\colon R\longrightarrow\kappa(\mathfrak p)
\]
be the canonical homomorphism. It induces the coefficientwise homomorphism
\[
 \lambda_{\mathfrak p,*}\colon R[[x,y]][Z]
 \longrightarrow\kappa(\mathfrak p)[[x,y]][Z],
 \qquad
 \sum a_{r,s,j}x^ry^sZ^j
 \longmapsto
 \sum \lambda_{\mathfrak p}(a_{r,s,j})x^ry^sZ^j.
\]
Set
\[
 P_{\mathfrak p}(Z;x,y)=\lambda_{\mathfrak p,*}\bigl(P(Z;x,y)\bigr).
\]
The associativity identity \eqref{eq:formal-associativity-resultant} and the
unit identities are coefficientwise polynomial identities. Applying
\(\lambda_{\mathfrak p,*}\) to both sides preserves these identities.
Consequently \(P_{\mathfrak p}\) is an associative formal \(n\)-valued
multiplication over \(\kappa(\mathfrak p)\) with a strong two-sided unit.
Moreover,
\(\kappa(\mathfrak p)\) has characteristic zero because \(R\) is a
\(\mathbb Q\)-algebra. Hence
\cref{cor:formal-field-commutativity} gives
\[
 P_{\mathfrak p}(Z;x,y)=P_{\mathfrak p}(Z;y,x).
\]

Comparing the coefficient of \(Z^{n-i}x^ry^s\) in this equality gives
\[
 \lambda_{\mathfrak p}(c_{i,r,s})=0.
\]
The kernel of \(\lambda_{\mathfrak p}\) is exactly \(\mathfrak p\), so
\(c_{i,r,s}\in\mathfrak p\). Since \(\mathfrak p\) was arbitrary,
\[
 c_{i,r,s}\in
 \bigcap_{\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec} R}\mathfrak p
 =\sqrt{(0)}.
\]
Thus every coefficient of \(P(Z;x,y)-P(Z;y,x)\) belongs to the nilradical of
\(R\). If \(R\) is reduced, then \(\sqrt{(0)}=0\), so all
\(c_{i,r,s}\) vanish and
\[
 P(Z;x,y)=P(Z;y,x).
\]
This proves \cref{thm:formal-commutativity}.
head: environment

label: eq:exp-relation
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Formal exponential independence

title: Proof
body_md:
Choose \(d\geq0\) so that every \(q_j\) has degree at most \(d\); such a bound
exists because there are only finitely many polynomials. Fix \(i\). Apply the
constant-coefficient differential operator
\[
 \mathcal{L}_i
 =\prod_{j\neq i}\left(\frac{\mathop{}\!\mathrm d}{\mathop{}\!\mathrm d T}-\alpha_j\right)^{d+1}
\]
to \eqref{eq:exp-relation}. For \(j\neq i\), the factor
\[
 \left(\frac{\mathop{}\!\mathrm d}{\mathop{}\!\mathrm d T}-\alpha_j\right)^{d+1}
\]
annihilates \(e^{\alpha_jT}q_j(T)\), because it becomes \(e^{\alpha_jT}q_j^{(d+1)}(T)\). Hence
\[
 e^{\alpha_iT}
 \prod_{j\neq i}
 \left(\frac{\mathop{}\!\mathrm d}{\mathop{}\!\mathrm d T}+\alpha_i-\alpha_j\right)^{d+1}
 q_i(T)=0.
\]
For a nonzero scalar \(c\in L\), the operator \(\mathop{}\!\mathrm d/\mathop{}\!\mathrm d T+c\) is invertible on the finite-dimensional vector space of polynomials of degree at most \(d\): in the monomial basis it is triangular with diagonal entry \(c\). Since \(\alpha_i-\alpha_j\neq 0\), the displayed product is injective on that space. Thus \(q_i=0\).
head: environment

label: eq:transport
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label[lemma]{lem:transport}
Let \((L,\partial_u)\) be a differential field of characteristic zero containing an element \(u\) with \(\partial_u u=1\). Let \(\lambda\in L\) satisfy \(\partial_u\lambda=0\), and let
\[
 w(u,v)\in \bigcup_{N\geq 1}L[[v^{1/N}]],
\]
where \(\partial_u\) acts coefficientwise. If
\begin{equation}\label{eq:transport}
 \partial_vw=\lambda\partial_uw,
 \qquad w(u,0)=u,
\end{equation}
then
\[
 w(u,v)=u+\lambda v.
\]
head: environment
name: A Puiseux solution of the transport equation

title: Proof
body_md:
Choose \(N\) such that
\[
 w(u,v)=u+\sum_{k\geq 1}c_kv^{k/N},
 \qquad c_k\in L.
\]
If some \(c_k\) with \(1\leq k<N\) were nonzero, choose the least such \(k\). The left-hand side of \eqref{eq:transport} would then have a nonzero term of \(v\)-order \(k/N-1<0\), whereas the right-hand side has no term of negative \(v\)-order. Hence \(c_k=0\) for \(k<N\).

Comparing the coefficient of \(v^0\) in \eqref{eq:transport} gives \(c_N=\lambda\). Subtract \(u+\lambda v\) from \(w\). If the remainder were nonzero, choose its least exponent \(k/N>1\). Differentiation with respect to \(v\) lowers this exponent by one, whereas coefficientwise differentiation with respect to \(u\) leaves it unchanged. The least \(v\)-orders on the two sides would therefore be different, a contradiction. Thus the remainder is zero.
head: environment

label: eq:iota
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label[lemma]{lem:ramified-evaluation}
Let \(C(t)\in K[[t]]\), let \(Q(t)\in tK[[t]]\) have linear coefficient \(1\), and put
\[
 q(s)=Q(s^m).
\]
Then the substitution
\begin{equation}\label{eq:iota}
 \iota\colon K[[x,y]]\longrightarrow K[[u,v]],
 \qquad x\longmapsto q(u),\quad y\longmapsto q(v),
\end{equation}
is injective.

Let \(L\) be a field containing \(K((u))\), and suppose that
\[
 \widehat z=q(u)+\delta,
 \qquad
 \delta\in v^{1/N}L[[v^{1/N}]]
\]
for some \(N\geq1\). Then \(C(\widehat z)\) is unambiguously defined by the Taylor expansion
\begin{equation}\label{eq:taylor-evaluation}
 C(\widehat z)
 =\sum_{j\geq0}\frac{C^{(j)}(q(u))}{j!}\delta^j
 \in L[[v^{1/N}]].
\end{equation}
The same convention respects sums, products, and composition of one-variable formal series whenever the indicated expressions are defined.
head: environment
name: Ramified substitution and evaluation

title: Proof
body_md:
Write \(U=u^m\) and \(V=v^m\). Substitution by \(Q\) is an isomorphism
\(K[[x,y]]\longrightarrow K[[U,V]]\), defined by
\(x\longmapsto Q(U)\) and \(y\longmapsto Q(V)\), because \(Q\) has a
compositional inverse in \(tK[[t]]\). The homomorphism
\[
 K[[U,V]]\longrightarrow K[[u,v]],
 \qquad U\longmapsto u^m,\quad V\longmapsto v^m,
\]
is injective. Its composite with the preceding isomorphism is
\eqref{eq:iota}.

Since \(q(u)\in u^mK[[u]]\), every coefficient \(C^{(j)}(q(u))\) belongs to \(K[[u]]\subset L\). Because \(\delta\) has strictly positive \(v\)-order, only finitely many summands in \eqref{eq:taylor-evaluation} contribute below any prescribed \(v\)-order. Thus the sum is a well-defined Puiseux power series. The compatibility with the ring operations and composition follows from the formal Taylor identities.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
\label[definition]{def:weak-unit}
Let \(X\) be an algebraic variety carrying an associative rational
\(n\)-valued multiplication. An element \(e\in X\) is a \emph{weak unit}
if the multiplication is defined at the generic points of
\(\{e\}\times X\) and \(X\times\{e\}\), and its restrictions satisfy
\[
 x\in e*x
 \qquad\text{and}\qquad
 x\in x*e
\]
for generic \(x\). It is a \emph{strong unit} if
\[
 e*x=x*e=\mathopen{[}x,\ldots,x\mathclose{]}.
\]
The variety \(X\) is called an \emph{algebraic \(n\)-valued monoid with a weak
unit} or an \emph{algebraic \(n\)-valued monoid with a strong unit},
respectively.
head: environment

label: eq:fermat-law
title: Example
body_md:
For simplicity, work over \(\mathbb C\), or over any algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. The Fermat curve gives a basic family. For \(n\geq2\), the polynomial
\[
 P(z;x,y)=z^n-x^n-y^n
\]
defines the commutative associative law (with an operation \(\ast_{\mathbb F_n}\))
\begin{equation}\label{eq:fermat-law}
 x*_{\mathbb F_n}y=
 \mathopen{[}
 \zeta_n^k\sqrt[n]{x^n+y^n}
 \mathbin{|} k=0,\ldots,n-1\mathclose{]}
\end{equation}
on \(\mathbb A^1\), where \(\zeta_n = e^{2\pi i/n}\). Both bracketings of three elements are the
roots of \(z^n=x^n+y^n+w^n\), each with the same multiplicity. Moreover,
\[
 0*_{\mathbb F_n}y=y*_{\mathbb F_n}0
 =\mathopen{[}\zeta_n^k y\mathbin{|}k=0,\ldots,n-1\mathclose{]}.
\]
Hence \(0\) is a weak unit, but it is not strong when \(n>1\).
head: environment

label: eq:polynomial-pullback
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Polynomial pullback

title: Proof
body_md:
Each value \(u\in T(a)*T(b)\) has \(m\) preimages under \(T\). On iterating
\eqref{eq:polynomial-pullback}, every value is therefore repeated once for
each preimage of the intermediate point. With multiplicities understood,
\[
 (a\circ_T b)\circ_T c
 =m\cdot\bigsqcup_{w\in (T(a)*T(b))*T(c)}T^{-1}[w]
\]
and
\[
 a\circ_T(b\circ_T c)
 =m\cdot\bigsqcup_{w\in T(a)*(T(b)*T(c))}T^{-1}[w].
\]
The two \(m^2n^2\)-multisets agree by associativity on \(X\). Since \(0\) is
a strong unit on \(X\),
\[
 0\circ_T y=y\circ_T0=n\cdot T^{-1}[T(y)].
\]
This multiset contains \(y\), so \(0\) is a weak unit. Commutativity follows
directly from the symmetry of \eqref{eq:polynomial-pullback} in \(a,b\).
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
The Fermat law \eqref{eq:fermat-law} is the polynomial pullback of ordinary
addition by \(T(z)=z^n\).
head: environment

label: thm:weak-unit-duality
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:weak-unit-duality}
Let \([u:v:w]\) denote the dual coordinates representing the line
\(ux+vy-wz=0\). For \(n\ge2\),
\[
 \{z^n-x^n-y^n=0\}^{\vee}
 =\{p_{n-1}(w^n;u^n,v^n)=0\}.
\]
The curve on the right encodes the \(n(n-1)\)-valued pullback law
\(\mathbb G_{n,n-1}\).
head: environment
name: Projective duality
